guide.summary: Cognition covers how we perceive, think, solve problems, remember, and measure intelligence. A recurring theme is that the mind uses efficient shortcuts that usually work but produce predictable errors: perceptual illusions, biased judgments, and reconstructed memories.

sections.heading: Perception
sections.body:
**Bottom-up processing** builds perception from sensory input; **top-down processing** uses expectations, schemas, and context. A **perceptual set** is a readiness to see what we expect.

**Gestalt principles** organize input into wholes: figure-ground, proximity, similarity, closure (filling gaps), continuity.

**Depth cues:** binocular (retinal disparity, convergence) need two eyes; monocular cues (relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, relative clarity) work with one.

**Selective attention** focuses on some input; **inattentional blindness** and **change blindness** show how much we miss.

sections.heading: Thinking and problem solving
sections.body:
**Algorithms** guarantee solutions but are slow; **heuristics** are fast shortcuts.

- **Availability heuristic:** judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind.
- **Representativeness heuristic:** judging by resemblance to a prototype, ignoring base rates.

Biases: **confirmation bias** (seeking supporting evidence), **framing** (wording changes choices: "90% survive" vs. "10% die"), **anchoring**, **overconfidence**, **functional fixedness**, **mental set**, **belief perseverance**, **hindsight bias**.

Creativity involves **divergent thinking** (many possible answers); **convergent thinking** narrows to one.

sections.heading: Memory
sections.body:
Memory involves **encoding**, **storage**, and **retrieval**. The multi-store model moves information from sensory memory to short-term/working memory (about 7 ± 2 items, seconds) to long-term memory. **Working memory** includes a central executive, phonological loop, and visuospatial sketchpad.

**Explicit** memories (episodic, semantic) depend on the hippocampus; **implicit** memories (procedural, priming, classical conditioning) involve the cerebellum and basal ganglia.

Improving memory: **deep (semantic) processing**, **spacing**, **testing effect**, **chunking**, mnemonics, and **encoding specificity**, including **context-dependent** and **state-dependent** memory.

Forgetting: **encoding failure**, decay, and **interference**: **proactive** (old blocks new) and **retroactive** (new blocks old). The **serial position effect** favors first (primacy) and last (recency) items.

Memory is **reconstructive**: the **misinformation effect** (leading questions alter recall) and **source amnesia** show how memories change. **Anterograde amnesia** blocks forming new memories; **retrograde** loses old ones.

sections.heading: Intelligence and testing
sections.body:
Theories: Spearman's **general intelligence (g)**, Gardner's multiple intelligences, Sternberg's triarchic theory. **Fluid intelligence** (reasoning speed) declines with age; **crystallized intelligence** (accumulated knowledge) holds or grows.

Good tests are **standardized** (normed on a representative group), **reliable** (consistent results), and **valid** (measure what they claim; predictive validity forecasts future performance). A test can be reliable without being valid. Scores form a **normal curve**: about 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD.

**Stereotype threat**, worrying about confirming a negative stereotype, can lower performance, raising fairness questions. **Achievement** tests measure learning; **aptitude** tests predict future ability.

keyTakeaways: Perception combines bottom-up input with top-down expectations.
Heuristics are efficient but produce predictable biases.
Memory is reconstructive and vulnerable to interference and misinformation.
Deep processing, spacing, and retrieval practice improve memory.
Reliability is consistency; validity is accuracy; reliability doesn't guarantee validity.
Fluid intelligence declines with age; crystallized holds.
commonMistakes: Mixing up proactive and retroactive interference.
Confusing availability (ease of recall) and representativeness (resemblance).
Calling anterograde amnesia the loss of old memories.
Treating a reliable test as automatically valid.
Confusing binocular and monocular depth cues.
Thinking memories are stored like recordings.
examTips: Scenario questions turn on the direction of interference or amnesia: ask "old or new?"
Normal curve questions require the 68–95–99.7 rule.
Recognize framing by comparing logically equivalent wordings.
On the EBQ, link each source to a named concept (misinformation effect, encoding specificity).
Watch for distractors that are real biases but don't match the scenario.

vocab.definition: Perception guided by expectations, knowledge, and context.
A mental predisposition to perceive one thing and not another.
A binocular depth cue based on the difference between the images in the two eyes.
Estimating likelihood based on how easily examples come to mind.
Judging likelihood by how well something matches a prototype.
Tendency to seek information that supports existing beliefs.
The way an issue is posed, which can significantly affect decisions.
Active processing of information in short-term memory.
Retrieval is best when cues present at encoding are present at retrieval.
Old information disrupts recall of new information.
New information disrupts recall of old information.
Incorporating misleading information into a memory of an event.
The consistency of a test's results.
The extent to which a test measures or predicts what it claims to.
Concern about confirming a negative stereotype, which can impair performance.

practice.stimulus: After watching several news reports about a plane crash, Ana decides to drive 800 miles instead of flying, even though driving that distance is statistically more dangerous.
practice.explanation: Vivid, easily recalled crash images inflate her estimate of flying's risk.

distractors.C: Representativeness involves matching to a prototype.

practice.stimulus: After surgery that damaged his hippocampus, a patient remembers his childhood clearly but cannot remember people he met after the surgery, even after many meetings.
practice.explanation: He can't form new explicit memories; old ones remain.

distractors.B: Retrograde amnesia is loss of memories from before the injury.

practice.stimulus: A logo consists of three curved line segments with gaps between them, but most viewers describe it as a circle.
practice.stem: Which Gestalt principle explains this perception?
practice.explanation: We fill gaps to perceive complete, whole objects.

distractors.B: Proximity groups items that are close together.

practice.stimulus: Participants hear a list of 20 words and then write down as many as they can. Recall is best for the first few and last few words.
practice.explanation: Primacy and recency produce a U-shaped recall curve.

practice.stimulus: At the start of the school year, Kenji keeps entering last year's locker combination when trying to open his new locker.
practice.explanation: Old information (last year's combination) interferes with new information.

practice.stimulus: Convinced that a new diet works, Rosa reads only online reviews from people who lost weight and dismisses studies showing no effect as poorly done.
practice.explanation: She seeks confirming evidence and discounts disconfirming evidence.

distractors.C: Hindsight bias is believing you knew it all along.

practice.stem: A person who has lost sight in one eye would still be able to use which depth cue?
practice.explanation: Linear perspective is a monocular cue; the others require two eyes.

practice.stimulus: A company's hiring test gives applicants nearly identical scores when they take it twice a month apart. However, scores don't correlate with employees' later job performance ratings.
practice.stem: The test is best described as
practice.explanation: Consistent scores show reliability; failure to predict performance shows low predictive validity.

distractors.B: A test can't be valid without some reliability, and this one is consistent.

practice.stimulus: Divers learned word lists either underwater or on land. They later recalled more words when tested in the same setting where they learned the list.
practice.explanation: The external environment served as a retrieval cue (encoding specificity).

distractors.B: State-dependent memory concerns internal states like mood or intoxication.

practice.stimulus: Compared with when she was 25, a 70-year-old woman is slower at solving novel logic puzzles but has a much larger vocabulary.
practice.stem: This pattern is best explained by

choices.text: a decline in fluid intelligence with stable or increasing crystallized intelligence

practice.explanation: Fluid reasoning tends to decline with age while accumulated knowledge persists.

distractors.B: Vocabulary is crystallized and has increased.

practice.stimulus: Before a difficult math test, one group of women is told the test has shown gender differences in the past; another group is told the test is gender-neutral. The first group scores significantly lower.
practice.stem: Which concept best explains the difference, and what does it imply about test scores?

choices.text: Stereotype threat; scores can reflect test conditions, not only ability.
Fluid intelligence; women have lower math aptitude.
Confirmation bias; the women sought confirming evidence.

practice.explanation: Activating a stereotype impaired performance, showing that situational factors affect measured ability.

distractors.B: The groups differ only in instructions, so ability differences can't explain the result.

practice.stimulus: Patients told that a surgery has a "90 percent survival rate" are much more likely to choose it than patients told it has a "10 percent mortality rate."
practice.stem: Which statement best explains this result?

choices.text: Logically equivalent information presented in different terms changes decisions, an example of framing.
The second group received worse medical information.
The availability heuristic made survival easier to imagine.
Patients in the first group experienced belief perseverance.

practice.explanation: The odds are identical; only the wording (gain vs. loss) differs.

practice.stimulus: Participants watched a video of a car accident. One week later, those asked "How fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?" were more likely than those asked about cars that "hit" each other to report seeing broken glass, though there was none.

choices.text: post-event information can alter memories, consistent with memory being reconstructive
memories are stored like video recordings
participants were lying to please the researcher

practice.explanation: The misinformation effect shows that wording after the event changed what people remembered.

practice.stimulus: An intelligence test is normed with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15, and scores are normally distributed.
practice.stem: About what percentage of people in the norming sample scored above 130?
practice.explanation: 130 is 2 SD above the mean. About 95 percent fall within 2 SD, leaving about 5 percent split between the tails: about 2.5 percent above.

practice.stimulus:
The three source summaries below were written for this practice set.

**Source A:** In a laboratory study, 150 participants watched a staged theft. Half were later asked a question implying the thief had a weapon; half were asked a neutral question. A week later, 32% of the misled group reported seeing a weapon, compared with 6% of the control group (p < .001).

**Source B:** Researchers reviewed lineup identifications made under controlled procedures (a lineup administrator who didn't know the suspect, immediate confidence statements). Witnesses who expressed high confidence at their first identification were correct about 90% of the time; low-confidence identifications were correct about 50% of the time.

**Source C:** In a study of 200 participants, people were more accurate at recognizing faces of their own racial group than faces of other groups (correct recognition 78% vs. 61%).
practice.prompt:
Using the sources, develop and justify an argument about whether eyewitness identifications should be relied on as strong evidence in criminal trials.

(a) Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.
(b)(i) Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.
(b)(ii) Explain how the evidence from part (b)(i) supports your claim using a psychological concept.
(c)(i) Support your claim using an additional piece of specific and relevant evidence from a different source.
(c)(ii) Explain how the evidence from part (c)(i) supports your claim using a different psychological concept.

rubric.description: A defensible claim, e.g., eyewitness identifications should be treated as strong evidence only when collected under controlled procedures and corroborated.
Cites specific evidence from one source (e.g., Source A: 32% vs. 6% reported a weapon after a leading question).

Explains how the evidence supports the claim using a psychological concept (e.g., the misinformation effect; memory is reconstructive). 1 point for naming/describing the concept accurately, 1 for linking it to the claim.
Cites specific evidence from a different source (e.g., Source C: 78% vs. 61% recognition; or Source B: 90% accuracy for initial high-confidence IDs under controlled procedures).
Explains with a different concept (e.g., the cross-race effect / encoding, or encoding specificity and how procedures reduce suggestion). 1 point for the concept, 1 for the link.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Eyewitness identifications should not be treated as strong evidence on their own; they are reliable only when gathered under controlled, non-suggestive procedures and should be weighed against factors known to distort memory.

(b)(i) In Source A, 32% of participants who were asked a leading question about a weapon later reported seeing one, compared with only 6% of those asked a neutral question.

(b)(ii) This demonstrates the misinformation effect: because memory is reconstructive, information introduced after an event can be incorporated into the memory itself. A witness questioned with suggestive wording by police or attorneys may sincerely recall details that never happened, so testimony collected after such questioning can't be treated as a reliable record of the event.

(c)(i) In Source C, participants correctly recognized 78% of faces from their own racial group but only 61% of faces from other groups.

(c)(ii) This reflects the cross-race effect, which arises at encoding: people process the distinguishing features of faces from familiar groups more deeply, so other-race faces are encoded less distinctively and are harder to recognize later. When a witness and suspect are of different races, the chance of misidentification rises, which is another reason identification alone shouldn't be decisive. Source B shows the problem can be reduced, since initial high-confidence identifications made under careful procedures were about 90% accurate, supporting reliance only when such procedures are followed.
